content: In 2013, eight out of 22 studies reported mixed results, showing both favorable and null associations between physical activity and health outcomes (Andersen et al., 2006; Duncan et al., 2006; Ness et al., 2007; Ortega et al., 2007; Dollman et al., 2010; Ruiz et al., 2011; Tudor-Locke et al., 2011; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c). Three studies reported only null associations (Ekelund et al., 2006; Hands et al., 2009; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012). One study reported a combination of favorable, null, and unfavorable associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a), while another study reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Hands and Parker, 2008). For vigorous physical activity (VPA), 10 out of 15 studies reported favorable associations (Ekelund et al., 2004; Lohman et al., 2006; Steele et al., 2009; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2010b; Mark and Janssen, 2011; Sayers et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2012; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a; Katzmarzyk et al., 2015b). Four studies reported mixed favorable and null associations (Ortega et al., 2007; Kelly et al., 2010; Belcher et al., 2010; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c), and one study reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Ortega et al., 2010). For moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), 20 out of 30 studies reported favorable associations (Ekelund et al., 2004; Lohman et al., 2006; Ness et al., 2007; Stevens et al., 2007; Mark and Janssen, 2009; Riddoch et al., 2009; Steele et al., 2009; Belcher et al., 2010; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2010b; Holman et al., 2011; Grydeland et al., 2012; Lawman et al., 2012; Carson et al., 2013; Ekstedt et al., 2013; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a; Taverno Ross et al., 2013; da Silva et al., 2014; Young et al., 2014; Katzmarzyk et al., 2015a; Katzmarzyk et al., 2015b). Six studies reported mixed favorable and null associations (Kelly et al., 2010; Peart et al., 2011; Ruiz et al., 2011; Mendoza et al., 2012; St George et al., 2013; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c). Three studies reported null associations (Hurtig-Wennlof et al., 2007; Ortega et al., 2007; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012), and one study reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Ortega et al., 2010). For moderate physical activity (MPA), two out of 10 studies reported favorable associations (Mark and Janssen, 2011; Chung et al., 2012). Two studies reported mixed favorable and null associations (Belcher et al., 2010; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c), while five studies reported null associations (Ortega et al., 2007; Steele et al., 2009; Sayers et al., 2011; Martinez-Gomez et al., 2012; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a). One study reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Ortega et al., 2010). No studies reported only unfavorable associations. For light physical activity (LPA), one out of nine studies reported favorable associations (Mark and Janssen, 2011). Two studies reported mixed favorable and null associations (Treuth et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2011). Three studies reported null associations (Ekelund et al., 2004; Sayers et al., 2011; Carson et al., 2013), and three studies reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Steele et al., 2009; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a; Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013c). For fat-free mass (FFM) and total physical activity, one out of two studies reported favorable associations (Ness et al., 2007), while the other reported mixed favorable and null associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a). For VPA, two out of four studies reported favorable associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a; Sayers et al., 2011), while the other two reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Lohman et al., 2006; Lohman et al., 2008). For MVPA, one out of four studies reported null associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a), while three reported mixed null and unfavorable associations (Lohman et al., 2006; Lohman et al., 2008; Taverno Ross et al., 2013). For MPA, both studies reported null associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a; Sayers et al., 2011). For LPA, one out of two studies reported favorable associations (Sayers et al., 2011), while the other reported mixed unfavorable (boys) and null (girls) associations (Jimenez-Pavon et al., 2013a). The quality of evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was downgraded from high to low due to serious risks of bias and indirectness. Non-randomized intervention studies were downgraded from low to very low due to similar concerns. Longitudinal studies were not upgraded due to serious risks of bias, and cross-sectional studies were downgraded to very low due to unexplained inconsistencies.
